scene.testo: The Allies asked Field Marshal Erich von Manstein about Marshal Zhukov. He gave a soldier's answer. Then he blamed one man in Berlin. Not Zhukov. Not the Red Army. Hitler. This is how that answer came to be.
Why would a general who won so many battles against the Red Army blame his own side? The answer sits in postwar records, memoirs, and a courtroom in Hamburg. But first, the question itself.
What did Manstein really think of Zhukov? And what did he say Hitler thought? The answer is short. But it explains how a brilliant German strategist ended the war in British captivity.
Summer 1945. Erich von Manstein is a British prisoner. Interrogators and historians want to know one thing from him. How did the Red Army, led by men like Zhukov, defeat the German army in the East?

Manstein was born in Berlin in 1887 as Fritz Erich von Lewinski. A childless aunt and her husband, Georg von Manstein, adopted him. He grew up inside the Prussian officer corps and became a staff officer.

In 1939, he was chief of staff to Army Group South in the Polish campaign. That winter, he pushed a bold plan for France. Strike through the Ardennes forest, not Belgium. The army high command repeatedly rejected it.

Hitler heard the idea in February 1940. He liked it. Manstein had been moved to an infantry corps, but a version of his plan became the plan. In May, German tanks crossed the Ardennes and reached the Channel coast.
Then came Russia. In 1941, Manstein led a panzer corps in the drive toward Leningrad. In September, he took over the 11th Army in the south. By autumn, his troops were fighting in the Crimea.

Crimea was a brutal assignment. Manstein's 11th Army had barely a dozen divisions, and the Perekop isthmus was a narrow bottleneck. In late October 1941, his troops broke through the Soviet defenses there and poured onto the peninsula.

In November, his forces swept across the peninsula. Soviet units fell back toward the naval base at Sevastopol. Only the fortress held. Manstein now faced a fortified port, with thick concrete, deep tunnels, and a determined garrison.

His first assault on Sevastopol began in December 1941. It failed. Soviet reinforcements arrived by sea, and a Red Army landing at Kerch in late December forced Manstein to divert troops east. The fortress got a reprieve.

In May 1942, Manstein struck first at Kerch. Operation Trappenjagd crushed the Soviet Crimean Front. Roughly 170,000 prisoners were reported taken. Only then could he turn his full strength back toward Sevastopol.

The siege guns arrived that June. Among them was the giant railway gun Dora, an 80-centimeter monster that fired shells weighing several tons. Its target was Fort Maxim Gorky, one of the strongest Soviet positions.

The bombardment began on June 2, 1942. For five days, German artillery and Luftwaffe bombers pounded the defenses. Then the infantry advanced. Fighting went fort by fort, tunnel by tunnel, often hand to hand.

Back in Moscow, Zhukov was far from Crimea. After the Moscow counteroffensive, he commanded the Western Front. In August 1942, Stalin named him Deputy Supreme Commander, making him the second-ranking figure in the Soviet war machine.
Stalin was demanding, and the men around him knew it. Zhukov was among the few who dared to argue with him. Soviet records show he often spoke bluntly to the dictator, and kept his post.

Meanwhile, Hitler's mood was shifting. The Moscow failure had shaken him. In December 1941, he sacked Brauchitsch and took direct command of the army himself. From then on, field commanders answered to a man who ruled from maps.

That role shaped everything Manstein would later write. Orders to hold ground at all costs became common. Retreat required permission, and permission was rarely granted. Manstein would call this the root of Germany's defeat.

On the ground in Crimea, the cost was high. The 11th Army lost heavily taking Sevastopol. Soviet defenders fought to the last in the coastal caves, and thousands of civilians and wounded were trapped there.

Manstein's own staff officer later recalled his icy calm during the offensive. He lived by the map and the clock. Subordinates described him as brilliant, but distant, and rarely willing to show warmth.

After Sevastopol, Hitler gave him new orders. The 11th Army was to move north against Leningrad. Manstein planned Operation Nordlicht, a heavy assault on the city, but Soviet attacks at Lake Ladoga disrupted the timetable.

In the Sinyavino battles of late summer 1942, Manstein's divisions threw back a Soviet attempt to break the Leningrad blockade. The city stayed encircled. Starvation continued inside, killing hundreds of thousands of civilians.
Here a darker side of the record appears. The 11th Army's area was also a zone of mass killing. Einsatzgruppe D operated in the south, murdering Jews, and the army supplied support and information.

In November 1941, Manstein issued an order to his troops that spoke of the Jewish-Bolshevik system and called for harsh measures. Historians cite it as evidence that the army shared Nazi aims in the East.

At Nuremberg, the prosecution later used this order. Manstein denied knowing about the killings. Yet the documents showed his headquarters worked closely with the units that carried them out. His defense never fully answered this.

Meanwhile, the strategic picture in the south was changing. Hitler launched Case Blue in summer 1942, sending Army Group South toward the Volga and the Caucasus oil fields. Two goals, one stretched front.

Zhukov watched this offensive from Moscow. Soviet planners had decided to hold, bleed the Germans in the cities, and prepare a massive trap. The plan was later called Operation Uranus, drawn up by Zhukov and Vasilevsky.
Autumn rains turned roads to mud. German units grew thin along the Don River. Many flank positions were held by Romanian, Italian, and Hungarian soldiers, poorly equipped for a heavy tank assault.

Manstein's 11th Army was still near Leningrad when the storm broke. On November 19, 1942, Soviet forces attacked the Romanian lines northwest of Stalingrad. Within days the pincers closed. Almost 300,000 men were trapped.

Inside the pocket, General Paulus appealed for permission to break out. Hitler refused. Goering promised that the Luftwaffe could supply the army by air. It was a promise the air fleet could not keep.

Manstein received his orders by telephone and teleprinter. Hitler's chief of staff, Zeitzler, urged a relief effort. The command was reshaped. A new Army Group Don would be created, and Manstein would lead it.

He left the Leningrad front in late November, traveling by train and aircraft across a frozen landscape. He reached his new headquarters at Novocherkassk with a hard choice ahead. Reach the trapped army, or save the whole southern front.

Meanwhile, a different kind of general was rising on the Soviet side. Georgy Zhukov had defeated the Japanese at Khalkhin Gol in 1939. In December 1941, his counteroffensive pushed German troops back from the gates of Moscow.

July 1, 1942. After a siege of roughly eight months, Manstein's army captured the fortress of Sevastopol. That same day, Hitler promoted him to field marshal. He was now one of the most famous commanders in the German army.
That autumn, Hitler sent him to the Stalingrad front. In November 1942, Soviet armies had surrounded the German 6th Army. Manstein took command of the new Army Group Don and was told to rescue it.
